result: Dog vaccination campaigns on Pemba Island from 2010-2014 achieved progressive improvements in coverage (from 13% in 2011 to 50% in 2014) and led to declining rabies incidence, with the effective reproduction number (Re) falling from ~1.5 in 2010 to <1 in 2014, and no cases detected from May 2014 to July 2016.
evaluation: Claims C53-C60 provide converging evidence from surveillance data, vaccination coverage estimates, and transmission modeling showing that improved dog vaccination led to rabies elimination by 2014. The temporal correlation between increasing vaccination coverage and declining incidence, combined with Re estimates falling below 1 and a 26-month period with no detected cases, strongly supports the conclusion of successful elimination.

result: Following a lapse in dog vaccination after 2014, two independent rabies virus introductions to Pemba in 2016 led to a major outbreak in 2016-2017, which was subsequently eliminated by October 2018 through reinstated island-wide dog vaccination campaigns achieving 61% median coverage.
evaluation: Claims C61-C68, C73-C74, and C106 collectively demonstrate outbreak re-emergence, response, and re-elimination. Phylogenetic evidence (C73-C74) confirms two independent introductions rather than undetected persistence, surveillance data documents the outbreak trajectory, and vaccination data shows the response. The causal link between vaccination lapse and outbreak spread (C106) is supported by both epidemiological and genomic evidence.

result: Integration of phylogenetic and epidemiological data resolved five distinct rabies transmission chains circulating on Pemba from 2010-2014, with approximately 54% (95% CI: 46.4-62.0%) of dog rabies cases detected during this period.
evaluation: Claims C69-C72 describe the phylogenetic analysis and case detection estimation. The methods for integrating genomic and epidemiological data are described in detail, and the case detection estimates are derived from transmission tree reconstruction with appropriate uncertainty quantification. The detection of 54% of cases is consistent with the intensive contact tracing described and provides confidence in the elimination assessment.

result: Case detection during the 2016-2018 outbreak was estimated at 69% (95% CI: 59.4-81.6%), representing 97 out of an estimated 140 rabid dogs.
evaluation: Claims C75-C76 report case detection estimates for the outbreak period using the same methodology as for 2010-2014. The higher detection rate during the outbreak is plausible given increased awareness and surveillance intensity. The estimates include appropriate uncertainty intervals and are consistent with the surveillance system described.

result: From 2010-2014, 45-72% of bite patients presenting to hospitals were bitten by probable rabid dogs, with 10-31 rabid bite victims estimated not to have received complete or timely PEP, and exposures receiving adequate PEP with probability 0.66-0.89.
evaluation: Claims C77-C82 describe PEP access during 2010-2014 using multiple lines of evidence: hospital surveillance data, contact tracing, modeling based on observed deaths, and triangulation with expected exposures from case detection estimates. The convergence of these independent estimates (C81) strengthens confidence in the findings. The probability estimates for PEP receipt are derived from empirical data.

result: During the 2016-2018 outbreak, 39 rabid bite victims did not obtain adequate PEP, exposures received appropriate PEP with probability 0.72-0.78, and probable exposures per rabid dog were higher (1.3) than in 2010-2014 (0.34-0.51), driven partly by variability in biting behavior including two dogs that each bit >10 people.
evaluation: Claims C83-C87 characterize PEP access and exposure patterns during the outbreak using contact tracing data. The estimates are derived using similar methods to the 2010-2014 period, allowing valid comparison. The identification of high-biting individuals (C87) is directly observed from contact tracing data and explains the higher exposure rate per rabid dog.

result: PEP access barriers changed over time: no shortages occurred during free provision (2011-2014), but cost barriers (~$12.9/vial) and shortages in late 2016 led to at least one child's death, prompting policy changes that improved awareness (17.5% to <4% unaware of PEP importance) and health worker counseling (20% to 3% not advised to obtain PEP).
evaluation: Claims C88-C94 document changes in PEP access barriers through surveillance data, case investigations, and contact tracing. The tragic case of the child who died due to PEP shortage (C90-C91) is well-documented and led to documented policy changes. The improvements in awareness and health-seeking behavior are quantified from contact tracing data comparing the two time periods.

result: The probability of rabies-exposed bite victims starting PEP increased from 0.667 (2010-2014) to 0.783 (2016-2020), and the probability of completing PEP increased from 0.397 to 0.84 over the same periods.
evaluation: Claims C95-C96 quantify improvements in PEP access and completion using contact tracing data. The substantial improvement in completion rates (0.397 to 0.84) is consistent with the documented policy changes (free PEP provision, improved awareness). These estimates are used in the decision tree model and are derived from empirical observations.

result: Over 11 years, approximately $17,800 was spent on PEP for 542 bite patients on Pemba, preventing around 42 rabies deaths (95% CI: 32-55) at a cost of approximately $424 per death averted, with intradermal regimens ($25) being substantially cheaper than intramuscular regimens ($56).
evaluation: Claims C97-C101 report cost and cost-effectiveness estimates based on compiled cost data and modeling. The cost estimates are derived from documented expenditures, and the deaths averted are estimated using established probability of rabies progression. The cost per death averted is calculated appropriately. However, the estimate relies on modeling assumptions about counterfactual scenarios.

result: Island-wide dog vaccination campaigns cost approximately $12,122 per campaign ($6.5 per dog vaccinated) and interrupted transmission within four years of implementation in both 2014 and 2018, but the lapse in vaccination from 2014 allowed two introductions in 2016 to spread widely.
evaluation: Claims C102-C106 report dog vaccination costs and effectiveness. The cost estimates are based on documented campaign expenditures. The claim that vaccination interrupted transmission within four years (C105) is supported by surveillance data showing no cases after May 2014 and after October 2018. The causal link between vaccination lapse and outbreak spread (C106) is supported by phylogenetic evidence showing the 2016 outbreak resulted from new introductions rather than undetected persistence.

result: Decision tree modeling over a 10-year horizon projected that: (1) status quo would result in 27 deaths; (2) PEP alone would prevent 48 deaths at $300/death averted but still result in 17 deaths; (3) dog vaccination with charged PEP would prevent 68 deaths at $1,684/death averted; and (4) combined dog vaccination with free PEP (One Health approach) would prevent 71 deaths at $1,657/death averted, resulting in only 4 deaths and preventing >300 exposures.
evaluation: Claims C107-C118 report results from a probabilistic decision tree model parameterized with empirical data from the study. The model structure is appropriate for comparing intervention scenarios, and parameters are derived from observed data (PEP access probabilities, case detection-adjusted incidence, biting behavior). Uncertainty is appropriately quantified with prediction intervals. The results are robust to discounting assumptions (C118). However, projections depend on model assumptions about future incidence patterns and intervention delivery.

result: Genomic data provided three key insights: (1) rabies was not circulating undetected from 2014-2016 but re-emerged due to external introductions; (2) two independent introductions occurred in 2016 rather than a single introduction; and (3) it is highly unlikely that other introductions after 2016 established onward transmission.
evaluation: Claims C145-C147 describe the value of genomic surveillance for distinguishing reintroduction from undetected persistence. The phylogenetic analysis (time-scaled phylogeny, discrete phylogeographic analysis) provides strong evidence for these conclusions. The identification of two distinct lineages in the 2016 outbreak, their phylogenetic placement relative to mainland sequences, and the lack of diversity in post-2016 sequences all support these inferences.

result: Despite high case detection, the study had limitations in reconstructing exact transmission pathways due to rabies virus's low mutation rate and short intervals between cases, though general transmission tree topology and plausible progenitors were identified with confidence, and key epidemiological estimates (Re, outbreak sizes) were robust to uncertainties.
evaluation: Claims C139-C143 acknowledge methodological limitations while asserting robustness of key findings. The acknowledgment of uncertainty in exact transmission links (C140) is appropriate given the low mutation rate of rabies. The claim of robustness for Re and outbreak size estimates (C142) is supported by sensitivity analyses using alternative pruning algorithms. The low sample recovery rate (~10-12%, C143) is a limitation but the authors demonstrate that key insights were still obtainable.

result: The cost per death averted for PEP on Pemba ($424, translating to $13 per DALY averted) is among the highest cost-effectiveness estimates from Gavi-eligible countries, resulting from the high proportion of bite patients presenting with rabies exposures rather than healthy dog bites, though cost-effectiveness declines in settings with more healthy dog bite presentations.
evaluation: Claims C149-C153 contextualize the cost-effectiveness findings. The comparison to other Gavi-eligible countries (C149) is supported by citation to Hampson et al., 2019. The explanation for high cost-effectiveness (C151) is logical and supported by the surveillance data showing 45-72% of bite patients were rabies exposures. The inference about declining cost-effectiveness in other settings (C152) is reasonable based on the model structure, though not directly tested.

result: While PEP is an essential emergency medicine, it does not address suffering from rabid animal injuries, is insufficient to protect the entire at-risk population, and faces access barriers from lack of awareness, expense, and supply issues; in contrast, mass dog vaccination reduces exposure risk, can achieve elimination, and remains extremely cost-effective compared to other health interventions despite higher cost per death averted than PEP.
evaluation: Claims C154-C159 synthesize findings about the complementary roles of PEP and dog vaccination. The limitations of PEP (C154-C156) are demonstrated by the study's findings on access barriers and deaths despite PEP availability. The advantages of dog vaccination (C157) are supported by the elimination achieved on Pemba. The cost-effectiveness comparison (C159) is supported by citation to Bertram et al., 2021 benchmarks. The higher cost per death averted for dog vaccination vs. PEP (C158) is shown in the modeling results.

result: This study is the first to confirm rabies elimination from an African setting through quantifying case detection and the first example of in-country whole-genome sequencing for rabies in Africa.
evaluation: Claims C22-C23 assert priority/novelty but are difficult to verify without comprehensive knowledge of all African rabies studies. The claim about confirming elimination through quantifying case detection (C22) is supported by the methods used, but whether this is truly the "first" in Africa requires verification against the literature. The claim about in-country sequencing (C23) is more verifiable from the methods description but still requires confirmation that no prior African studies performed in-country rabies whole-genome sequencing.

result: The transferability of cost-effectiveness estimates from Pemba is limited because elimination may take longer and be more fragile in denser, more connected populations, though costs per dog vaccinated may be lower in larger populations; the estimates lie within expectations for sub-Saharan Africa but require better quantification of the relationship between vaccination coverage and risk reduction, and research on health-seeking behaviors.
evaluation: Claims C160-C166 appropriately discuss limitations in generalizability and identify research needs. The inferences about challenges in denser populations (C160) and economies of scale (C161) are reasonable extrapolations. The acknowledgment that estimates lie within regional expectations (C162) is supported by citation. The identification of research needs (C164-C165) is appropriate given the uncertainties in the model. The discussion of stochastic variation and implementation fidelity (C166) is supported by the study's own experience with vaccination lapses.

result: The authors conclude that a One Health approach to rabies (combining dog vaccination with free PEP access) is very cost-effective and can bring rapid success, with lessons from Pemba building confidence in the feasibility of elimination elsewhere in Africa while highlighting the importance of sustaining commitment and coordinating dog vaccination over large scales.
evaluation: Claims C168-C171 represent the authors' main conclusions, which are well-supported by the study's findings. The cost-effectiveness of the One Health approach (C168) is demonstrated by the modeling results. The feasibility of elimination (C169) is demonstrated by achieving it twice on Pemba. The importance of sustained commitment (C170) is illustrated by the outbreak following vaccination lapse. The need for large-scale coordination (C171) is a reasonable inference from the reintroduction events, though this extrapolation goes beyond what was directly tested.

result: The introduction establishes the global rabies burden (59,000 annual deaths), the preventability through PEP and dog vaccination, the success of elimination in high-income countries and Latin America, the lack of investment in Africa and Asia, the 'Zero by 30' elimination goal, and the challenges including sparse vaccination campaigns, rapid coverage decline, weak surveillance, and very few documented elimination examples in Africa (only four locations, all with subsequent re-establishment).
evaluation: Claims C1-C19 provide background context supported by appropriate citations to established literature. The global burden estimate (C1), transmission patterns (C2), clinical characteristics (C3), and prevention methods (C4-C5) are well-established facts. The regional disparities (C6), global goals (C7), and implementation challenges (C8-C13) are supported by cited sources. The literature review identifying only four African elimination examples with subsequent re-establishment (C14-C17) provides important context, though the completeness of this review cannot be fully verified.

result: Pemba Island is 988 km² in area, located 50 km from mainland Tanzania, comprises four districts with 121 villages, had a projected 2020 population of 438,765, with a very high human:dog ratio (~118:1), almost all dogs unconfined, and 10-20% unowned.
evaluation: Claims C24-C30 describe the study site characteristics. Geographic and administrative data (C24-C26) are factual. The population projection (C27) is appropriately cited to census data. The human:dog ratio (C28) and dog ownership patterns (C29-C30) are based on study data. These descriptive claims provide essential context for interpreting the results.

result: The study used records from January 2010 to January 2021 for contact tracing, obtained 16 near whole-genome sequences from Pemba (8 previously published, 8 new), and published 14 previously unpublished whole-genome sequences from mainland Tanzania (2009-2017).
evaluation: Claims C31-C35 describe the data sources and are straightforward methodological statements. The time period of data collection (C31), number of sequences (C32), and publication status (C33-C35) are factual statements about the study's data. These are verifiable from the methods section and supplementary materials.

result: Dog vaccination on Pemba began with a small campaign in 2010 (705 dogs), followed by four annual island-wide campaigns (2011-2014) as part of a demonstration project, with post-vaccination transects in 2013-2014 to estimate coverage; PEP was provided free during the demonstration project (2011-2014) with training in intradermal and intramuscular administration, but patients were charged $12.9/vial after 2015 until the government reinstated free provision in 2017 following the 2016 outbreak.
evaluation: Claims C36-C45 describe the intervention history and are factual statements about program implementation supported by documentation and citations. The vaccination campaign details (C36-C39), PEP provisioning policies (C40-C42), and outbreak response (C43-C45) provide essential context for interpreting the epidemiological results. These claims are descriptive rather than analytical.

result: The vaccination coverage model used a pup-to-adult ratio (PAR) of 0.256 from Serengeti District data, assumed mean vaccine-induced immunity duration of 3 years, and used an annual dog death rate of 0.595.
evaluation: Claims C46-C48 describe model parameters. The PAR estimate (C46) is appropriately sourced from a comparable setting (Serengeti District) with proper citation. The vaccine immunity duration assumption (C47) of 3 years is reasonable for rabies vaccines. The death rate (C48) is cited to appropriate literature. These parameter choices are justified, though some involve assumptions that could affect results.

result: All Pemba sequences grouped within the RABV minor clade Cosmopolitan-AF1b; an exploratory dataset of 244 publicly available sequences from this clade was obtained from RABV-GLUE; TempEst analysis showed moderate temporal signal (R²=0.37); and Bayesian discrete phylogeographic analysis was conducted on 153 Tanzanian genomes including 13 from the 2016/17 Pemba outbreak.
evaluation: Claims C49-C52 describe phylogenetic methods and preliminary analyses. The clade assignment (C49) is based on standard methods. The dataset assembly (C50) is appropriate for contextualizing Pemba sequences. The temporal signal assessment (C51) shows moderate but sufficient signal for molecular clock analysis (R²=0.37 is acceptable for phylogeographic inference). The phylogeographic analysis design (C52) is appropriate for addressing the study questions.

result: The discussion contextualizes findings within broader rabies metapopulation dynamics, noting that despite Pemba's isolation, considerable RABV diversity arose from historical introductions, the rapid 2016 outbreak spread highlights elimination fragility, reintroduction risks remain high while rabies is uncontrolled in nearby populations, and examples from Latin America show dramatic contractions when dog vaccination is scaled up and sustained.
evaluation: Claims C119-C125 synthesize the study's findings with broader literature. The metapopulation dynamics framework (C119) is supported by citations. The interpretation of Pemba's viral diversity (C120) is consistent with the phylogenetic results. The inference about elimination fragility (C121) is demonstrated by the study's own findings. The discussion of reintroduction risks (C122-C123) is supported by multiple citations. The Latin America examples (C124-C125) provide useful comparative context with appropriate citations.

result: The discussion contrasts Pemba's intensive contact tracing with weak routine surveillance in Africa, notes that low case detection leads to underestimation and difficulty ascertaining elimination, describes how high case detection on Pemba generated confidence in elimination, compares to more intensive approaches in high-income countries, notes the tractability of contact tracing given low bite patient incidence, and discusses the potential value of contact tracing and genomic surveillance for rabies elimination programs.
evaluation: Claims C126-C138 discuss surveillance implications. The contrast with weak African surveillance (C126) is supported by citation. The consequences of low case detection (C127) are logical inferences. The confidence from high detection (C128) is supported by the case detection analysis. The comparison to high-income countries (C129-C130) is appropriately cited. The feasibility discussion (C131-C133) is based on study experience. The recommendations for contact tracing (C135) and genomic surveillance (C138) are reasonable extrapolations, though somewhat speculative.

result: The COVID-19 pandemic highlights how disruption can severely set back rabies programmes.
evaluation: Claim C167 is supported by three citations documenting COVID-19 impacts on rabies programs. This provides relevant context about the vulnerability of rabies control programs to disruption, reinforcing the importance of sustained commitment discussed elsewhere in the paper.
